fields.meaning: With the intention of, intending to
examples: I meant it as a joke, but I ended up hurting him.
I'm studying English with the intention of studying abroad.
I'm saving that money as if I had spent it on drinks.
I checked the inside of the store as if I were a customer.
I gave my opinion believing I was right, but it provoked resentment.
I took notes intending not to forget.
fields.explain:
Placed before the main action as an adverbial expressing intention/purpose.
Vたつもりで often goes with verbs of saving/substitution:貯金する・我慢する・控える.
When emphasizing a stance/role: Nのつもりで + an action of observing/evaluating.
Usually subjective; if the purpose is clearly objective, use ～ために.

• States the purpose/intention when performing the main action: “with the intention of …, …”.
• Vたつもりで: “acting as if … had been done, in order to …”, used for saving/substitution.
• Nのつもりで: “playing the role of / assuming one is …”.
• Subjective nuance; differs from ～ために (actual purpose) because it emphasizes “mindset/tendency”.
fields.notes:
• N3–N2. Often appears in reading questions when stating “playing the role of a customer/target”.
• Vたつもりで has a nuance of “restraint, substitution” that is very typical in savings ads/slogans.
• The comma can be omitted in short sentences: 冗談のつもりで言ったが…
mistakes: Used as a predicate: ～つもりで。× → A main clause must follow.
Confusing it with ～ために: if it shows a subjective mindset → つもりで; if an objective purpose → ために.
Vたつもりで does not mean the action was actually done; many trick questions state “not done, but treated as done”.
Wrong combination: Naだのつもりで × → Naなつもりで ○; Nだのつもりで × → Nのつもりで ○

examples: You cannot enter until your ID has been checked.
Traffic cannot pass until the construction work is finished.
I can't decide until I've talked it over with my parents.
You can't drink alcohol until you turn 20.
This software cannot be used until it has been installed.
fields.explain:
Used in rules, instructions and warnings: ～ません／～できません follows.
The clauses can be reordered to emphasize the procedure:予約してからでないと、受付できません。
Its nuance is more formal/standard than ordinary ないと/なければ because it emphasizes “only after having…”.

• States a necessary condition before carrying out the following action/accepting the following state: “Only after V can…”.
• The main clause usually means “cannot/not allowed/difficult”; it is rarely a direct affirmative.
• Expresses a mandatory sequence, rules, procedures, safety logic.
fields.notes:
• The main clause is almost always negative/expresses difficulty: ～ない／できない／困る／無理だ.
• Useful in legal/procedural contexts: 入場、登録、承認、確認、支払い など.
• “じゃないと” is a colloquial variant; avoid it in formal documents. | Variant: ～てからでなければ
mistakes: Using an affirmative main clause: ×登録してからでないと利用できます → it should be 利用できません.
Confusing the time sequence: the Vて clause is a condition that must be completed first; avoid describing simultaneous actions.
Missing conditional logic: the first clause must be a feasible/controllable action.
Confusing it with て初めて: てからでないと is a mandatory necessary condition; て初めて is a first-time realization/result.

examples: Try this. It's good.
Try it once more. You should be able to do it.
Try reading it out loud.
Go outside and try feeling the wind.
Try thinking about it yourself.
It's dangerous, so why don't you try not touching it? (sarcastic)
fields.explain:
Used only with subordinates/children/people you are close to; not used with superiors/customers.
“～て ごらんなさい ” sounds softer than “～て ごらん ”.
Same function as “～てみなさい”; “～てみる” is voluntary and does not carry a command.
It can sound somewhat imposing if the relationship is not close enough.

• A suggestion/mild command, “try doing … and see”, directed at a listener of lower status or in a close relationship.
• Carries a nuance of encouraging direct experience: trying it to feel/conclude for oneself.
• ～てごらん is an imperative variant of “ご覧になる/ごらん” (to look/see), extended to all verbs via Vて.
fields.notes:
• Originates from “ご覧なさい” (look!), extended into a mild command pattern for all verbs via Vて.
• In marketing/apps: “まずは無料で試してごらん” sounds quite casual; in standard writing, “お試しください” should be used.
• The interrogative form “～てごらん？” carries a nuance of invitation or sarcasm depending on intonation.
mistakes: Using it with superiors/customers: inappropriate. Use “～てください／～ていただけますか”.
Confusing it with “～てみる”: ～てごらん is a command; ～てみる is trying something yourself.
Using the negative “～ないでごらん” in the wrong place can easily sound sarcastic/unpleasant.
Forgetting the polite form “～てごらんなさい” in educational/parent-child contexts.

examples: I can't stop worrying about tomorrow's results.
I'm terribly envious of him.
I can't go out because of the rain, and I'm bored to death.
I'm worried sick about my child.
I'm dying to see you soon.
My feet are unbearably itchy.
fields.explain:
Leans toward colloquial use; used in everyday conversation to emphasize a strong degree.
Usually carries negative emotions; positive emotions are also possible but less common.
“で(は)” after な/N adds emphasis:退屈 では しょうがない (more emphatic than退屈でしょうがない).
Avoid using it to describe objective states/things that are not emotions (×忙しくてしょうがない in the objective sense of having a lot of work; use it only when the speaker feels “miserable because of being busy”).

Expresses a very strong degree of emotion/sensation, “unbearable/hard to stand”, almost beyond control.
• Usually used for spontaneous emotions: うれしい、悔しい、心配だ、恥ずかしい、退屈だ…
• The subject is usually the speaker (or someone whose feelings the speaker can empathize with/sense).
• Colloquial nuance. “～でしょうがない” sounds strongly conversational, while “～しょうがありません” is formal.
• Negative: ～なくてしょうがない (会えなくてしょうがない: not being able to see someone makes me terribly restless).
fields.notes:
• “しょうがない” = “仕方がない” (colloquial). In formal written language, prefer “仕方がない/しょうがありません”.
• Often appears in fixed phrases: 気になってしょうがない／心配で(は)しょうがない／退屈で(は)しょうがない。
• When the subject is someone else, a context that allows inference about their feelings is usually needed.
mistakes: Wrong form combination: ×嬉しいでしょうがない → 嬉しくてしょうがない; ×静かでしょうがない → 静かで(は)しょうがない.
Describing objective facts instead of the speaker's emotions → unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with ～でならない (more formal) and ～でたまらない (stronger).
JLPT N2: often tests conjugation (くて/で/て) and distinguishing the three patterns ～しょうがない／～たまらない／～ならない.

examples: It was only after getting sick that I realized how important health is.
Only after having children did I understand how hard my parents had worked.
Only after living alone did I learn how hard housework is.
Only after going on a business trip abroad did I keenly feel the need for English.
Only when you get sick do you understand how important health is.
Only after the teacher pointed it out did I notice my own mistake.
fields.explain:
After ～てはじめて comes a clause of result/first-time realization:分かった／気づいた／実感した／始まる…
Not used for ordinary, repeated results; it emphasizes “for the first time (初めて)”.
Often accompanied by words indicating a first time:初めて; はじめて itself already includes “first time”.
Narrative/reflective nuance; often seen in written language, essays, interviews.

• Meaning: “Only after/when doing X, for the first time…”, emphasizing that it had not happened/not been realized before.
• Scope: Usually goes with a result clause that is a first-time discovery/realization/feeling, or a state that starts to take effect.
• Implied negation of what came before: it implies “not before that” (まだ/全然/分からなかった…).
• Pivotal point in time: X is the trigger point for Y. Not used for obvious everyday things.
fields.notes:
• After ～てはじめて, the verb is usually one of perception: 分かる／気づく／感じる／実感する／認識する／始める.
• Useful for skillfully stating a lesson learned from experience in reflective essays: 「失敗してはじめて、改めるべき点が見えた。」
• Do not attach a particle for a specific point in time before はじめて (×昨日してはじめて); use a Vて clause to indicate the turning point.
mistakes: Using it with a result that is not a “first time/realization” → wrong nuance. Replace it with ～てから.
Stating an obvious event/one without a trigger-result relationship → unnatural.
Confusing it with ～て以来 (continuing) in JLPT questions: watch for signals like “until now/ずっと”.
Wrong tense: using Vた + はじめて (×) → it must be Vてはじめて.

fields.explain: ◎ Accepting being told or thought of in that way, even though it is not the best outcome.

meaning_vi: Expresses the feeling of accepting an unsatisfactory result.

I have no choice but to go
2. ②　電車が止まったのなら、遅れても仕方（が）ない。

fields.connection: V (plain form) + ということ / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい
examples: According to the people at the ryokan, there are cold days here even in summer.
According to this morning's news, a famous writer passed away yesterday.
fields.explain: ◎ I will tell you what I have learned from information such as people's stories and what I have read.

examples: According to the long-range forecast, this summer is going to be hot.
According to the doctor, I would probably be able to leave the hospital in about two months.
I hear the area around Tokyo Station used to be sea long ago.
"I heard on the news that JR fares are going to be raised next year."
"There was a phone call a little while ago saying that Yamada-san will be absent today."
"I hear your daughter passed her university entrance exam. Congratulations."
fields.explain:
Used for hearsay: conveying indirect information from newspapers, other people, or official announcements.
Used to summarize or interpret a conclusion after presenting a situation.
Neutral, objective nuance; does not emphasize personal emotions.
In spoken language, it can be used to end a sentence when explaining: “…ということだね”.
Not suitable for commands or personal volition.

～ということだ has two main interpretations depending on the context:
• Conveying information/hearsay: “I hear that…”, “it is reported that…”. The speaker did not witness it directly but relays information from another source.
• Conclusion/interpretation: “that is…”, “that means…”, used to sum up what has just been stated.
In both cases, this pattern has an objective nuance, shows little personal emotion, and is common in written language, news, and logical explanations.
fields.notes:
1) The two meanings of ～ということだ are easily confused.
→ It means “I hear that…” (hearsay) and “that is…” (explanation/definition).
2) Look at the context.
→ If there is a source/something heard: the meaning is “I hear that”.
→ If summarizing or restating: the meaning is “that is”.
3) Easily confused with ～って (colloquial).
→ ～ということだ is more formal and often used in written language. | Spoken variant: ～ってことだ
mistakes: Confusing it with ～そうだ: if the sentence expresses a conclusion/summary, ～そうだ is not used.
Confusing it with ～わけだ: ～わけだ has a subjective nuance, while ～ということだ is more neutral.
Using it for personal volition: wrong. Example: ❌ 行きたいということだ.
Incorrectly omitting 「だ」 with nouns/na-adjectives in standard written language.
In JLPT reading, if the sentence contains “according to the newspaper, according to the announcement”, choose ～ということだ first.

Speaking of summer vacation, my family went on a trip every year.

fields.explain:
Placed after a noun/topic just heard or seen, to open an association or ask for clarification.
Often goes with verbs of association:思い出す・連想する・言えば…
When confirming meaning, というと is usually followed by a question/explanation clause.
It feels more casual than といえば in direct conversation; というと leans toward “typical association”.

• Association/typical: from a keyword, states what is commonly associated, a representative example.
• Checking/re-emphasizing content: used when you want to confirm “if you say that, it means…, right?”.
• Conversational nuance; というと emphasizes a topic shift triggered by a keyword just mentioned/heard.
fields.notes:
• Often appears in conversation when hearing a new keyword: A「留学します。」B「留学というと、どこに？」
• というと is not used to define concepts; for definitions use というのは／とは.
• In written language, というと often goes with formulaic phrases: 一般に～といえば／～と聞くと～を連想する。
mistakes: Using というと to connect two clauses with no association → forced. There should be a clear reminder relationship.
Confusing it with というのは for definitions. というと is not used to define terms.
Confusing the nuance with といったら: というと is neutral; といったら carries strong/excessive emotion.

examples: 「肉じゃが」 is a dish of meat, potatoes, onions and so on simmered together.
The Coming-of-Age Ceremony is an event celebrating turning 20.
「おもてなし」 means a heart that is considerate of others.
Tokyo is a city where people and information come together.
I can't go. That's because something urgent has come up.
Saying that he is a genius is a bit of an exaggeration.
fields.explain:
After というのは there is usually a sentence giving a definition, stating the essence, or making a general evaluation.
When used to give a reason, the following sentence often ends with からだ／ためだ／わけだ to make the causal relationship clear.
More formal than っていうのは; suitable for documents and lectures.
It can also be used with a clause: S(plain) + というのは、～ (the fact that … is …).

• Defining/explaining a concept: AというのはBだ = “what is called A is B”.
• Introducing a reason: place というのは at the beginning of the sentence that follows, to state the reason for the previous sentence.
• Explanatory, coherent nuance; often used in presentations, writing, or when you want to clarify a term.
fields.notes:
• Since it gives a definition, avoid an overly specific example right after というのは; state the essence first, then give examples.
• When giving a reason, というのは usually comes at the beginning of a sentence, starting a new one after a period or a paragraph break.
• In negative evaluations, it often goes with ～にすぎない／～とは限らない／～わけではない.
meaning_vi: Defines what something is like. The meaning of ~ is...
examples: 1. ➀　デジカメとは
デジカメ is...
2. ②　デジカメとは、デジタルカメラ（のこと）だ。
デジカメ is a digital camera.
3. ③　「ひそひそ話すって（いうのは）、どんな話し方？」「ほかの人に聞こえないように小さい声で話すことだよ」
"What kind of way of talking is whispering?" "It's talking in a low voice so that other people can't hear."
4. ➃　顔が広いと（いうの）は、いろいろな分野に友達がたくさんいるという意味だ。
Having a wide circle of acquaintances means having many friends in various fields.
Definition variant: N + とは
mistakes: Using というと instead of というのは to define → wrong function.
Forgetting は: “多様性というのは” → without は, the meaning is incomplete in its defining role.
Turning というのは into a long-winded bridge between two sentences that have no reason/definition relationship → wordy, loses coherence.
